explanations.explanation: A great famine, friend. The text says, “So there was a great famine in Samaria.” (2 Kings 6:25) Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had marched his whole army up to besiege the city. The siege went on so long that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver.

The text doesn't mention a plague. It says, “So there was a great famine in Samaria.” (2 Kings 6:25) The trouble was hunger, because Ben-hadad, king of Aram, besieged the city so long. A donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver.

No shaking ground in this one. The text says the city was besieged so long that there was a great famine (2 Kings 6:25). Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had marched up with his entire army. I think that was a hard stretch for the people of Samaria.

True. The text says a quarter cab of dove's dung sold for five shekels of silver (2 Kings 6:25). That's a small measure of something nobody wants in their kitchen, and it still cost silver. I think that tells you exactly how hard things had gotten.

It's true, actually. The text says a quarter cab of dove's dung sold for five shekels of silver (2 Kings 6:25). I know, I read it twice too. I think it shows how hard the siege had gotten, when even that was bought and sold.

True. The king answers her, “If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you?” (2 Kings 6:27) Then he adds a question about the threshing floor and the winepress. I think that's a king who is looking at empty hands.

The text says it plainly. The king answers, “If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you?” (2 Kings 6:27) He doesn't promise her anything. Then he asks whether help could come from the threshing floor or the winepress.

He tears his clothes. The text says, “When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes.” (2 Kings 6:30) As he passed by on the wall, the people saw the sackcloth under his clothes, right next to his skin. I think this part of the story hurts.

explanations.answer: He sends for the other woman
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say he sends for her. It says he heard the woman's words and tore his clothes (2 Kings 6:30). As he passed by on the wall, the people saw the sackcloth underneath. This is a heavy moment, friend, and I think the king felt it.

The text never mentions storehouses being opened. What it says is that the king tore his clothes when he heard her words (2 Kings 6:30). Sackcloth was underneath, and the people saw it. It's a heavy part of the story, and I think it hit him hard.

explanations.answer: Shut the door to keep him out
explanations.explanation: Shut the door! Elisha, the prophet, tells the elders, “…when the messenger comes, shut the door to keep him out.” (2 Kings 6:32) He already knows what the messenger is coming for. I'd say Elisha's door policy that day was very clear.

explanations.answer: Open the door and welcome him
explanations.explanation: No welcome mat at this house. Elisha, the prophet, tells the elders, “…when the messenger comes, shut the door to keep him out.” (2 Kings 6:32) He had just said the king sent someone to cut off his head. I think a shut door was the friendliest thing on offer.

explanations.answer: Send him back with an answer
explanations.explanation: The text has Elisha keep the messenger out instead. Elisha, the prophet, tells the elders, “…when the messenger comes, shut the door to keep him out.” (2 Kings 6:32) No message goes back at that point. The door does the talking.

True. Elisha asks, “Is not the sound of his master’s footsteps behind him?” (2 Kings 6:32) The messenger was sent by the king, so his master's footsteps coming right behind him means the king himself is close. Elisha sees it all coming before it shows up at the door.

It's true. Elisha, the prophet, asks, “Is not the sound of his master’s footsteps behind him?” (2 Kings 6:32) The messenger was sent by the king, so that master is the king. Elisha says he can hear him coming right behind the messenger.

It's the other way around. The king says, “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (2 Kings 6:33) He is asking why he should keep waiting. I think that's a man running out of patience, friend.

False is right. The king says, “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (2 Kings 6:33) He's asking why he should keep waiting. I think he's run out of patience, and that's exactly where Elisha's next words land.

explanations.answer: Food will be cheap and plentiful
explanations.explanation: Cheap and plentiful, friend! A seah of fine flour for one shekel, and two seahs of barley for one shekel (2 Kings 7:1). Compare that to a donkey's head at eighty shekels of silver. That's quite a drop, and Elisha says it's coming about this time tomorrow.

Elisha says the opposite. This is what the LORD says: a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel (2 Kings 7:1). That's tiny money next to eighty shekels for a donkey's head. The prices are about to drop, and fast.

explanations.answer: Only the king's household will eat
explanations.explanation: The text puts these prices at the gate of Samaria, where the sales happen (2 Kings 7:1). It never limits them to the king's household. A seah of fine flour for a shekel is a price for the whole city to see.
Eat. Elisha says, “You will see it with your own eyes…” and then, “but you will not eat any of it.” (2 Kings 7:2) The officer gets a front row seat and no cookie. I mean, no flour.

Not sell. Elisha says, “You will see it with your own eyes…” and then, “but you will not eat any of it.” (2 Kings 7:2) The officer had asked if the LORD making windows in heaven could really make this happen. He gets to watch it, and the eating is not for him.

Share is a good guess, but the word is eat. Elisha says, “You will see it with your own eyes…” and then, “but you will not eat any of it.” (2 Kings 7:2) The officer is going to watch the whole thing happen. He just won't get a bite.

explanations.answer: Over to the camp of the Arameans
explanations.explanation: To the Aramean camp! The four men say, “So come now, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:4) Staying put means dying and going into the city means dying. So they take the one option that has a maybe in it.

The Jordan isn't where they head. The four men say, “So come now, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:4) Their plan was to walk right up to the army that had Samaria surrounded. That takes some nerve.

explanations.answer: Down to the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up in their plan. The four men say, “So come now, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:4) They set out at twilight (2 Kings 7:5). Sometimes the answer is closer than you think.

That's not what they find. The text says that at the outskirts of the camp, “…there was not a man to be found.” (2 Kings 7:5) No sleeping soldiers, no guards. I bet those four were braced for snoring and got silence.

False is right. The text says that when they came to the outskirts of the camp, “…there was not a man to be found.” (2 Kings 7:5) No soldiers sleeping and no soldiers awake. Imagine walking up ready for the worst and finding an empty lot.

explanations.answer: Chariots and horses and a great army
explanations.explanation: That's it. The Lord had caused the Arameans to hear “…the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army…” (2 Kings 7:6) The Arameans said to one another that the king of Israel must have hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians to attack them. They took it from there.

explanations.answer: The walls of Samaria cracking apart
explanations.explanation: Cracking walls? Not in this story, friend. The Lord had caused the Arameans to hear “…the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army…” (2 Kings 7:6) That sound alone had them running for their lives (2 Kings 7:7).

explanations.answer: Trumpets blowing from the city gate
explanations.explanation: No trumpets in this one. The Lord had caused the Arameans to hear “…the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army…” (2 Kings 7:6) That's the sound the text gives, and it's enough to empty a camp.

Tents and animals, all of it. The text says they ran, “…abandoning their tents and horses and donkeys.” (2 Kings 7:7) When people run for their lives, they don't stop to pack. The four men walked into a camp with everything still in place.

The text doesn't mention broken chariots. It says the Arameans fled, “…abandoning their tents and horses and donkeys.” (2 Kings 7:7) They left a whole lot more than that behind. The camp was ready for whoever walked in.

They left much more than that. The text says, “The camp was intact, and they had run for their lives.” (2 Kings 7:7) They abandoned their tents and horses and donkeys. The four men found a camp that looked like everyone had just stepped out.

True. After hiding the first load, the text says they entered another tent, carried off some items from there, and hid them (2 Kings 7:8). They had gone into the first tent to eat and drink, and then carried off silver, gold and clothing. I think a person in that spot can lose track of how many trips they've made.

It's true, they went back for more. The text says that on returning, they entered another tent, carried off some items from there, and hid them (2 Kings 7:8). That's a second tent and a second load. I think the whole situation was a lot to take in.

explanations.answer: We are not doing what is right
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news.” (2 Kings 7:9) With their loot hidden, they stop and say it out loud to each other. They also say that if they wait until morning light, their sin will overtake them.

explanations.answer: We should take it all before dawn
explanations.explanation: They go the other direction. They say, “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news.” (2 Kings 7:9) They also say that if they wait until morning light, their sin will overtake them. They decide to stop and tell somebody.

explanations.answer: We should leave before they return
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have them worrying about that. They say, “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news.” (2 Kings 7:9) They also say that if they wait until morning light, their sin will overtake them. Their minds are on the city, not on running.

The king's household. They say, “Now, therefore, let us go and tell the king’s household.” (2 Kings 7:9) These are men who had been sitting at the entrance of the city gate. They call out to the gatekeepers, and the gatekeepers shout the news until it's reported to the king's household (2 Kings 7:10-11).

Elisha isn't who they say they'll tell. They say, “Now, therefore, let us go and tell the king’s household.” (2 Kings 7:9) The text names the king's household as their audience. They go to the city gatekeepers first, and the news travels from there.

The text names a different group. The four men say, “Now, therefore, let us go and tell the king’s household.” (2 Kings 7:9) They call out to the gatekeepers, who shout the news along (2 Kings 7:10-11). That's how it travels all the way inside.

explanations.answer: Left camp to hide and ambush them
explanations.explanation: That's what the king thinks. He tells his servants, “They know we are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the field…” (2 Kings 7:12) He expects them to take the Israelites alive and walk into the city. An empty camp looked like a trap to him.

explanations.answer: Gone home to bring more soldiers
explanations.explanation: The king doesn't say that. He tells his servants the Arameans know they are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the field (2 Kings 7:12). He thinks they plan to take the Israelites alive when they come out. He's expecting a trap.

explanations.answer: Left the camp as a peace offering
explanations.explanation: Not at all, friend. The king tells his servants, “They know we are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the field…” (2 Kings 7:12) He's thinking of an ambush, where they take the Israelites alive when they come out. Nothing about peace in that.

explanations.answer: Everyone left in the city is doomed anyway
explanations.explanation: That's his argument. The servant says, “Their plight will be no worse than all the Israelites who are left here. You can see that all the Israelites here are doomed.” (2 Kings 7:13) If the scouts are in trouble, they're in no more trouble than everyone else. So let's send them and find out.

explanations.answer: The horses are too weak to carry riders
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The servant says, “Their plight will be no worse than all the Israelites who are left here. You can see that all the Israelites here are doomed.” (2 Kings 7:13) That's his reason for sending them. Nothing about the horses being weak.

explanations.answer: The Arameans never attack in the dark
explanations.explanation: The servant never says anything like that. He says, “Their plight will be no worse than all the Israelites who are left here. You can see that all the Israelites here are doomed.” (2 Kings 7:13) His point is that waiting won't save anybody either. So he says, let's send them and find out.

The road was anything but clean. The text says the whole way was littered with the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown off in haste (2 Kings 7:15). The scouts followed it as far as the Jordan. That's a trail you can't miss.

False is right. The text says the scouts tracked them as far as the Jordan, and the whole way was littered with the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown off in haste (2 Kings 7:15). It looked like a very hurried departure. That's proof enough for the scouts to bring back to the king.

True. The text says, “Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:16) After the scouts reported, the whole city could finally go out the gate. After all that hunger, they headed straight for the camp.

It's true, they did. The text says, “Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:16) The scouts had brought back word, and the people went out to the camp. The city that had been shut in finally got out.

explanations.answer: It drops just as Elisha said
explanations.explanation: Down it goes, exactly as promised. The text says a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, “…according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Kings 7:16) That's the very price Elisha announced. Same price, same gate.

explanations.answer: It stays as high as before
explanations.explanation: Still as high as before? Not a chance, friend. The text says a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, “…according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Kings 7:16) Compare that to a donkey's head at eighty shekels of silver. The price Elisha, the prophet, announced is the price that came.

explanations.answer: It doubles by the next morning
explanations.explanation: Doubling? Friend, the price went the other direction! The text says a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, “…according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Kings 7:16) That's exactly what Elisha, the prophet, had said. The LORD's word did not miss by a single shekel.

explanations.answer: The people trample him and he dies
explanations.explanation: Yes, and I'll say it once: this part is heavy. The text says the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died, just as the man of God had foretold (2 Kings 7:17). Elisha had told him, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!” (2 Kings 7:2) The LORD's word held, every bit of it.

explanations.answer: He eats the first flour from the camp
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Elisha said. He told the officer, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!” (2 Kings 7:2) The text says the people trampled the officer in the gateway, and he died (2 Kings 7:17). It's a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: He chases the Arameans to the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says. The king had appointed him to be in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died (2 Kings 7:17). That's what Elisha had foretold. It's a heavy part of the story.
